bull_thesis: First, the identity: ticker 9927 in Hong Kong is Seres Group (the Huawei-partnered maker of the premium AITO / Wenjie electric SUVs; A-shares are 601127 in Shanghai), not Leapmotor as the peer file states. Every hard number in the scan matches Seres. The bull case is a balance-sheet-first, deep-value one. At HK$42.08 the whole company is worth roughly RMB 63-70 billion, and it holds about RMB 59.75 billion of net cash (cash of RMB 64.1bn against just RMB 4.4bn of debt at March 31, 2026). Strip the cash out and the market is paying almost nothing for a business that did RMB 165 billion of revenue and RMB 5.96 billion of net profit in 2025 and threw off about RMB 12.6 billion of trailing free cash flow -- plus a 10% stake in Huawei's smart-car unit Yinwang (RMB 11.5bn at cost, with option value if Yinwang ever lists) and the owned AITO trademark (about RMB 2.5bn). The half-year 2026 loss is blamed on cyclical input costs -- memory-chip prices up roughly five-fold and lithium carbonate up about 125% -- not on the customer walking away; NEV deliveries still grew ~3.9% in the half. If those commodity costs normalize and AITO's refreshed line-up (the new M9, M8 and M6) plus overseas expansion restore mid-single-digit net margins on ~RMB 160bn of revenue, normalized earnings power is RMB 5-8 billion. Put a conservative 8-10x on that, add the Yinwang stake and a realistic slice of the cash, and the parts are worth meaningfully more than today's price. The stock is down nine straight months, near its 52-week low, and the H-share already trades near where a bearish analyst pegs the usually-pricier A-share -- a washed-out setup where the assets are real and the earnings only need to stop deteriorating.
bear_thesis: The 2024-25 profit turn was a thin, cost-sensitive spread on a product Seres does not really own -- and the first serious cost shock erased it. A company that posted a RMB 754 million profit in the first quarter pre-announced a first-half loss of RMB 1.5-1.8 billion ten weeks later, meaning the second quarter alone was disastrous (the AITO subsidiary lost RMB 1.9-2.15bn in the quarter). That is not a premium franchise with pricing power; it is an assembler with no margin shock-absorber. Demand is cracking alongside costs: June 2026 volume fell 28.1% year over year, and the company wrote down assets already made obsolete by a brutal product cycle. The moat is largely rented from Huawei, which is actively multiplying its partner brands (Avatr, Luxeed, Stelato, Maextro) -- each one dilutes AITO's exclusivity and Huawei's incentive to favor Seres, while Huawei keeps the software and brand economics. The 'net cash' is partly an illusion of automaker working-capital float (large supplier payables that are not counted as debt), plus fresh IPO proceeds already earmarked (70% for R&D) and the remaining Yinwang installment -- so it is not freely distributable and is not a hard floor. There is no dated catalyst to force a re-rating: the only near-term event is the late-August interim result, which will simply confirm the loss. consensus_delta: Where we might disagree with the street: on an enterprise-value basis (the roughly RMB 63-70bn market value minus RMB 59.75bn of net cash) the market is paying close to nothing for a franchise that earned RMB 5.96bn in 2025, generated ~RMB 12.6bn of trailing free cash flow, AND owns a RMB 11.5bn stake in Huawei's Yinwang unit -- arguably too harsh if the 2026 cost spike (memory chips up ~5x, lithium up ~125%) proves cyclical. interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Seres Group Co., Ltd. (9927.HK, H-shares)

**Prepared as of 2026-07-17. Live price HK$42.08 (prior close HK$45.22 — the figure carried in the screener scan). Fundamentals reported in Chinese yuan (RMB); the quote is in Hong Kong dollars (HKD). Conversion used: 1 RMB ≈ 1.09 HKD.**

> **Identity correction — read first.** The screener scan left the company name blank, and the peer-comps file for this ticker names it "Zhejiang Leapmotor." That is wrong. Ticker 9927 on the Hong Kong exchange is **Seres Group Co., Ltd. — H shares** (the Huawei-partnered maker of the AITO / Wenjie premium electric vehicles; A-shares trade in Shanghai as 601127). Leapmotor is a different company (9863.HK). Every hard number in the scan matches Seres, not Leapmotor: 2024 revenue of RMB 145.2 billion, first-ever annual profit of RMB 5.95 billion, and the jump from RMB 35.8 billion of revenue in 2023 are Seres's figures exactly — Leapmotor did roughly RMB 32 billion of revenue in 2024. The rest of this dossier treats the name as Seres.

> **Evidence note.** No earnings-call transcript was bundled, and our licensed transcript feed is not subscribed for this name. This dossier therefore cross-references management's *public* statements — the July 13, 2026 profit warning, the April 30, 2026 first-quarter release, and the November 2025 listing prospectus — against the hard financials in the scan. No quotes are invented; where I could not source a claim I say so.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Seres is one of the most violent boom-and-bust stories in the China electric-vehicle complex. For most of its life (as Chongqing Sokon) it was a loss-making minivan and small-car maker. The story changed completely when it became Huawei's flagship manufacturing partner for the AITO ("Wenjie") brand — premium, Huawei-software-defined SUVs. The AITO M9, a vehicle priced above RMB 500,000, became the best-selling model in its class in China through 2024. That drove the revenue explosion visible in the scan: from RMB 35.8 billion (2023) to RMB 145.2 billion (2024) to RMB 165.1 billion (2025), and the first profits in the company's history (RMB 5.95 billion in 2024, RMB 5.96 billion in 2025).

The company then did two things that define today's setup. First, in November 2025 it listed H-shares in Hong Kong at HK$131.50, raising about HK$14.3 billion — the largest carmaker listing in Hong Kong in four years, with roughly US$8.3 billion of cornerstone demand. Second, it bought a 10% stake in Huawei's smart-car unit, Shenzhen Yinwang Intelligent Technology, for RMB 11.5 billion, and acquired the AITO trademark from Huawei for about RMB 2.5 billion — an attempt to own more of the value chain rather than rent all of it.

The arc has since inverted hard. The stock is down about 61% this year and roughly 68% from its November listing price, and management on July 13, 2026 warned of a first-half loss. The narrative has flipped from "Huawei's profit engine" to "sells more, loses more."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management's claim / public position | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Premium franchise with real pricing power (AITO as "China's #1 luxury NEV brand," per its own Brand Finance citation) | 2024–25 net margin was thin for a "premium" maker — 3.6% net in 2025 — and it *collapsed into a loss* in Q2 2026 the moment input costs rose. Gross margin 29.1% in 2025 but not defended. | Poorer than the story — the margin is fragile, not premium-durable |
| Growth is intact (Q1 2026 revenue +34.5% to RMB 25.75bn; NEV unit sales +43.9%) | True for Q1, but H1 total vehicles fell ~1% YoY to 196,580 and **June sales fell 28.1% YoY**. Momentum reversed within the half. | Matched early, then broke |
| "Ample cash reserves and a sound balance-sheet structure" (July 13 warning) | Verified: net cash of about RMB 59.75bn (cash RMB 64.13bn vs total debt RMB 4.38bn) at March 31, 2026. This is the strongest part of the story. | Verified |
| The half-year loss is a cost shock, not a demand problem | H1 2026 loss of RMB 1.5–1.8bn (vs +RMB 2.94bn a year earlier) is blamed on memory-chip prices up ~5x, lithium carbonate up ~125%, and asset write-downs. But June volume −28% says demand also softened. | Partly true — cost is the headline, but demand is cracking too |
| Capital allocation is building an ecosystem asset (Yinwang stake, AITO trademark) | Real cash out the door — RMB 11.5bn for 10% of Yinwang, ~RMB 2.5bn for the trademark. Strategic, but it consumed a large slice of the cash the balance-sheet story rests on. | Real, but reduces the "free" cash |

The core tension: the revenue and the 2024–25 profit turn are genuine, but the profitability proved to be a **thin, cost-sensitive spread on a Huawei-defined product** rather than a durable premium margin. The first serious input-cost shock erased two years of margin progress in a single quarter.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining.** Without call transcripts I read tone from the cadence of disclosures. The November 2025 prospectus and the April 2026 Q1 release were offensive in posture — record IPO, new-model launches (the all-new M9 pre-sale, the M6 with "10,000 orders in 15 minutes"), overseas-expansion spend. By the July 13, 2026 warning the language turned defensive and balance-sheet-first ("ample cash reserves," "sound balance-sheet structure," "short-term profitability impacted by rising raw-material costs"). The shift from talking about growth and orders to reassuring on solvency is the classic offensive-to-defensive rotation.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Low-to-Medium, and freshly damaged.** The company does not give tight numeric guidance in the Western sense, so I judge credibility by the gap between the confident Q1 framing (revenue +34%, sales +44%) and the H1 outcome (a loss and a ~1% volume decline for the half). A company that reported a RMB 754 million Q1 profit on April 30 pre-announced a first-half *loss* ten weeks later — meaning Q2 was catastrophic (the AITO subsidiary alone lost RMB 1.9–2.15bn in the quarter). The speed of that reversal is the single most credibility-damaging fact here. The one claim I can independently corroborate — the strong net-cash position — is verified, which is why credibility is not lower than it is.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The pressure points the market is pressing on, and where management has been thin:
- **Structural margin.** Is Seres a premium brand or a contract assembler for Huawei that keeps a thin slice? The Q2 loss argues the latter. Management has not credibly answered this.
- **Huawei dependence and value capture.** Huawei now spreads the same smart-car technology across a stable of partners (Avatr, Luxeed with Chery, Stelato with BAIC, Maextro with JAC). Each new sibling brand dilutes AITO's exclusivity and Huawei's incentive to favor Seres. Management frames the Yinwang stake as alignment; skeptics read it as paying Huawei for a seat it cannot afford to lose.
- **The cash question.** How much of the RMB 59.75bn net cash is genuinely free versus working-capital float owed to suppliers, plus the remaining Yinwang installment and the R&D spend the IPO earmarked (70% of proceeds)? Management leads with the gross figure and does not bridge to distributable cash.
- **Citi (analyst Jeff Chung)** cut the A-share target to RMB 37.40 from RMB 55.40 in July 2026 and kept a Sell rating — the street is not giving the recovery the benefit of the doubt.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 A Q1 profit (RMB 754m) flipping to a pre-announced H1 loss (−RMB 1.5–1.8bn) within ten weeks — margin has no shock absorber.
🔴 June 2026 unit sales −28.1% YoY — the demand side is weakening at the same time as costs, not just costs alone.
🔴 Asset write-downs for models/assets "limited by technological iteration" — an admission that recent capital spending is aging faster than expected in a brutal product cycle.
🔴 Rented moat: the brand's appeal and the intelligent-driving stack belong substantially to Huawei, which is actively multiplying its OEM partners.
🔴 Stock down nine consecutive months; H-share IPO buyers (Nov 2025, HK$131.50) are down ~68% — a demoralized, potentially forced shareholder base.
🟢 Genuine net cash of ~RMB 59.75bn against a market value of roughly RMB 63–70bn — the balance sheet is a real cushion, unusual for a China EV maker.
🟢 A strategic 10% Yinwang stake (RMB 11.5bn at cost) and the owned AITO trademark — real assets with option value if Yinwang ever lists.
🟢 The cost drivers (memory, lithium) are cyclical commodity/component prices that can normalize; the loss is not (yet) a demand-collapse story alone.
🟢 AITO deliveries still grew modestly in H1 (NEV units +3.9%), so the franchise has not lost the customer outright.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The pivot in disclosure language from "orders and launches" to "balance-sheet resilience" is the tell that management expects a rough few quarters, not a one-print blip.
- Buying the trademark and a Yinwang stake *before* the downturn hit suggests management sensed its dependence on Huawei was a strategic vulnerability — the "Seres can no longer rely solely on Huawei" theme in the Chinese press predates the crash.
- The H-share now trades near, and arguably below, the level Citi assigns the A-share (RMB 37.40) — for a dual-listed name where the A-share usually trades at a *premium*, the H-line is priced for something close to the bear case already.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a genuinely cheap balance sheet wrapped around an earnings engine whose durability was just disproven. The net cash and the Yinwang stake are real and large relative to the market value — on an enterprise-value basis (market value minus net cash) the market is paying almost nothing for the auto business plus the Yinwang stake. That is the entire bull case. Against it: there is no dated catalyst forcing a re-rating, the operating trend is still worsening (June volume −28%, Q2 subsidiary loss ~RMB 2bn), and the margin proved to be a thin, cost-sensitive spread on a product Seres does not fully own.

**Moat:** narrow and eroding. The AITO franchise is real but substantially *rented* from Huawei, whose expanding partner roster and control of the software/brand economics cap Seres's structural margin — a high-2024/25-margin that fell to a loss on the first cost shock is an eroding position, not a durable one. **Moat trend: eroding.** **Secular threat: material (not terminal)** — the structural risk is Huawei-ecosystem value capture plus the China NEV price war compressing the whole cohort, which impairs the *level* of Seres's terminal margin without extinguishing the franchise. None of the house's named secular-decline themes fits cleanly; this is an intra-industry margin-capture and price-war risk. The cheapness is therefore a genuine fear-print on the assets, but sitting on an earnings base whose normalized power is now unproven — closer to a "cheap on assets, unproven on earnings" situation than a clean mispricing.

No quotes are invented; where I could not source a claim I say so.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Seres is one of the most violent boom-and-bust stories in the China electric-vehicle complex. For most of its life (as Chongqing Sokon) it was a loss-making minivan and small-car maker. The story changed completely when it became Huawei's flagship manufacturing partner for the AITO ("Wenjie") brand — premium, Huawei-software-defined SUVs. The AITO M9, a vehicle priced above RMB 500,000, became the best-selling model in its class in China through 2024. That drove the revenue explosion visible in the scan: from RMB 35.8 billion (2023) to RMB 145.2 billion (2024) to RMB 165.1 billion (2025), and the first profits in the company's history (RMB 5.95 billion in 2024, RMB 5.96 billion in 2025).

The company then did two things that define today's setup. First, in November 2025 it listed H-shares in Hong Kong at HK$131.50, raising about HK$14.3 billion — the largest carmaker listing in Hong Kong in four years, with roughly US$8.3 billion of cornerstone demand. Second, it bought a 10% stake in Huawei's smart-car unit, Shenzhen Yinwang Intelligent Technology, for RMB 11.5 billion, and acquired the AITO trademark from Huawei for about RMB 2.5 billion — an attempt to own more of the value chain rather than rent all of it.

The arc has since inverted hard. The stock is down about 61% this year and roughly 68% from its November listing price, and management on July 13, 2026 warned of a first-half loss. The narrative has flipped from "Huawei's profit engine" to "sells more, loses more."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management's claim / public position | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Premium franchise with real pricing power (AITO as "China's #1 luxury NEV brand," per its own Brand Finance citation) | 2024–25 net margin was thin for a "premium" maker — 3.6% net in 2025 — and it *collapsed into a loss* in Q2 2026 the moment input costs rose. Gross margin 29.1% in 2025 but not defended. | Poorer than the story — the margin is fragile, not premium-durable |
| Growth is intact (Q1 2026 revenue +34.5% to RMB 25.75bn; NEV unit sales +43.9%) | True for Q1, but H1 total vehicles fell ~1% YoY to 196,580 and **June sales fell 28.1% YoY**. Momentum reversed within the half. | Matched early, then broke |

| The half-year loss is a cost shock, not a demand problem | H1 2026 loss of RMB 1.5–1.8bn (vs +RMB 2.94bn a year earlier) is blamed on memory-chip prices up ~5x, lithium carbonate up ~125%, and asset write-downs. But June volume −28% says demand also softened. | Partly true — cost is the headline, but demand is cracking too |

The core tension: the revenue and the 2024–25 profit turn are genuine, but the profitability proved to be a **thin, cost-sensitive spread on a Huawei-defined product** rather than a durable premium margin. The first serious input-cost shock erased two years of margin progress in a single quarter.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining.** Without call transcripts I read tone from the cadence of disclosures. The November 2025 prospectus and the April 2026 Q1 release were offensive in posture — record IPO, new-model launches (the all-new M9 pre-sale, the M6 with "10,000 orders in 15 minutes"), overseas-expansion spend. By the July 13, 2026 warning the language turned defensive and balance-sheet-first ("ample cash reserves," "sound balance-sheet structure," "short-term profitability impacted by rising raw-material costs"). The shift from talking about growth and orders to reassuring on solvency is the classic offensive-to-defensive rotation.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Low-to-Medium, and freshly damaged.** The company does not give tight numeric guidance in the Western sense, so I judge credibility by the gap between the confident Q1 framing (revenue +34%, sales +44%) and the H1 outcome (a loss and a ~1% volume decline for the half). A company that reported a RMB 754 million Q1 profit on April 30 pre-announced a first-half *loss* ten weeks later — meaning Q2 was catastrophic (the AITO subsidiary alone lost RMB 1.9–2.15bn in the quarter). The speed of that reversal is the single most credibility-damaging fact here. The one claim I can independently corroborate — the strong net-cash position — is verified, which is why credibility is not lower than it is.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The pressure points the market is pressing on, and where management has been thin:
- **Structural margin.** Is Seres a premium brand or a contract assembler for Huawei that keeps a thin slice? The Q2 loss argues the latter. Management has not credibly answered this.
- **Huawei dependence and value capture.** Huawei now spreads the same smart-car technology across a stable of partners (Avatr, Luxeed with Chery, Stelato with BAIC, Maextro with JAC). Each new sibling brand dilutes AITO's exclusivity and Huawei's incentive to favor Seres. Management frames the Yinwang stake as alignment; skeptics read it as paying Huawei for a seat it cannot afford to lose.
- **The cash question.** How much of the RMB 59.75bn net cash is genuinely free versus working-capital float owed to suppliers, plus the remaining Yinwang installment and the R&D spend the IPO earmarked (70% of proceeds)? Management leads with the gross figure and does not bridge to distributable cash.
- **Citi (analyst Jeff Chung)** cut the A-share target to RMB 37.40 from RMB 55.40 in July 2026 and kept a Sell rating — the street is not giving the recovery the benefit of the doubt.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 A Q1 profit (RMB 754m) flipping to a pre-announced H1 loss (−RMB 1.5–1.8bn) within ten weeks — margin has no shock absorber.
🔴 June 2026 unit sales −28.1% YoY — the demand side is weakening at the same time as costs, not just costs alone.
🔴 Asset write-downs for models/assets "limited by technological iteration" — an admission that recent capital spending is aging faster than expected in a brutal product cycle.
🔴 Rented moat: the brand's appeal and the intelligent-driving stack belong substantially to Huawei, which is actively multiplying its OEM partners.
🔴 Stock down nine consecutive months; H-share IPO buyers (Nov 2025, HK$131.50) are down ~68% — a demoralized, potentially forced shareholder base.
🟢 Genuine net cash of ~RMB 59.75bn against a market value of roughly RMB 63–70bn — the balance sheet is a real cushion, unusual for a China EV maker.
🟢 A strategic 10% Yinwang stake (RMB 11.5bn at cost) and the owned AITO trademark — real assets with option value if Yinwang ever lists.
🟢 The cost drivers (memory, lithium) are cyclical commodity/component prices that can normalize; the loss is not (yet) a demand-collapse story alone.
🟢 AITO deliveries still grew modestly in H1 (NEV units +3.9%), so the franchise has not lost the customer outright.

- The pivot in disclosure language from "orders and launches" to "balance-sheet resilience" is the tell that management expects a rough few quarters, not a one-print blip.
- Buying the trademark and a Yinwang stake *before* the downturn hit suggests management sensed its dependence on Huawei was a strategic vulnerability — the "Seres can no longer rely solely on Huawei" theme in the Chinese press predates the crash.
- The H-share now trades near, and arguably below, the level Citi assigns the A-share (RMB 37.40) — for a dual-listed name where the A-share usually trades at a *premium*, the H-line is priced for something close to the bear case already.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a genuinely cheap balance sheet wrapped around an earnings engine whose durability was just disproven. The net cash and the Yinwang stake are real and large relative to the market value — on an enterprise-value basis (market value minus net cash) the market is paying almost nothing for the auto business plus the Yinwang stake. That is the entire bull case. Against it: there is no dated catalyst forcing a re-rating, the operating trend is still worsening (June volume −28%, Q2 subsidiary loss ~RMB 2bn), and the margin proved to be a thin, cost-sensitive spread on a product Seres does not fully own.

- **The cash question.** How much of the RMB 59.75bn net cash is genuinely free versus working-capital float owed to suppliers, plus the remaining Yinwang installment and the R&D spend the IPO earmarked (70% of proceeds)? Management leads with the gross figure and does not bridge to distributable cash.
- **Citi (analyst Jeff Chung)** cut the A-share target to RMB 37.40 from RMB 55.40 in July 2026 and kept a Sell rating — the street is not giving the recovery the benefit of the doubt.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 A Q1 profit (RMB 754m) flipping to a pre-announced H1 loss (−RMB 1.5–1.8bn) within ten weeks — margin has no shock absorber.
🔴 June 2026 unit sales −28.1% YoY — the demand side is weakening at the same time as costs, not just costs alone.
🔴 Asset write-downs for models/assets "limited by technological iteration" — an admission that recent capital spending is aging faster than expected in a brutal product cycle.
🔴 Rented moat: the brand's appeal and the intelligent-driving stack belong substantially to Huawei, which is actively multiplying its OEM partners.
🔴 Stock down nine consecutive months; H-share IPO buyers (Nov 2025, HK$131.50) are down ~68% — a demoralized, potentially forced shareholder base.
🟢 Genuine net cash of ~RMB 59.75bn against a market value of roughly RMB 63–70bn — the balance sheet is a real cushion, unusual for a China EV maker.
🟢 A strategic 10% Yinwang stake (RMB 11.5bn at cost) and the owned AITO trademark — real assets with option value if Yinwang ever lists.
🟢 The cost drivers (memory, lithium) are cyclical commodity/component prices that can normalize; the loss is not (yet) a demand-collapse story alone.
🟢 AITO deliveries still grew modestly in H1 (NEV units +3.9%), so the franchise has not lost the customer outright.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The pivot in disclosure language from "orders and launches" to "balance-sheet resilience" is the tell that management expects a rough few quarters, not a one-print blip.
- Buying the trademark and a Yinwang stake *before* the downturn hit suggests management sensed its dependence on Huawei was a strategic vulnerability — the "Seres can no longer rely solely on Huawei" theme in the Chinese press predates the crash.
- The H-share now trades near, and arguably below, the level Citi assigns the A-share (RMB 37.40) — for a dual-listed name where the A-share usually trades at a *premium*, the H-line is priced for something close to the bear case already.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a genuinely cheap balance sheet wrapped around an earnings engine whose durability was just disproven. The net cash and the Yinwang stake are real and large relative to the market value — on an enterprise-value basis (market value minus net cash) the market is paying almost nothing for the auto business plus the Yinwang stake. That is the entire bull case. Against it: there is no dated catalyst forcing a re-rating, the operating trend is still worsening (June volume −28%, Q2 subsidiary loss ~RMB 2bn), and the margin proved to be a thin, cost-sensitive spread on a product Seres does not fully own.

**Moat:** narrow and eroding. The AITO franchise is real but substantially *rented* from Huawei, whose expanding partner roster and control of the software/brand economics cap Seres's structural margin — a high-2024/25-margin that fell to a loss on the first cost shock is an eroding position, not a durable one. **Moat trend: eroding.** **Secular threat: material (not terminal)** — the structural risk is Huawei-ecosystem value capture plus the China NEV price war compressing the whole cohort, which impairs the *level* of Seres's terminal margin without extinguishing the franchise. None of the house's named secular-decline themes fits cleanly; this is an intra-industry margin-capture and price-war risk. The cheapness is therefore a genuine fear-print on the assets, but sitting on an earnings base whose normalized power is now unproven — closer to a "cheap on assets, unproven on earnings" situation than a clean mispricing.
